content: Dentistry is practiced differently across the world, with variations in training and professional requirements depending on the country. Dentistry in Australia Dentistry in Australia is regulated by the Australian Dental Association, while specialization is overseen by the Royal Australasian College of Dental Surgeons. Dentists trained in Australia must meet the entry requirements of accredited institutions offering dental courses and complete full-time academic training to earn a dental degree. Those wishing to specialize must pursue additional study after gaining clinical experience. To practice dentistry in Australia, registration is required in the specific state where the dentist intends to work, and registration requirements vary by state. Generally, only individuals holding qualifications such as BDS, BDSc, or BDent from Australian or New Zealand universities are eligible for registration. Foreign graduates must meet additional requirements, including residency, an employment visa, passing the Australian Dental Council (ADC) examinations, or completing a two-year advanced standing program to obtain a locally accredited qualification. Universities such as Adelaide, Melbourne, Queensland, Western Australia, La Trobe, and Griffith offer five-year undergraduate dental programs, while Sydney University offers a four-year graduate entry program requiring a prior bachelor's degree. Charles Sturt University and James Cook University began offering dental programs in 2009. The qualifications from these institutions meet the academic requirements for registration with all Australian Dental Boards. Dentistry in New Zealand Dentistry in New Zealand is regulated by the New Zealand Dental Association, with specialization overseen by the Royal Australasian College of Dental Surgeons. The University of Otago is the only dental school in New Zealand, offering the required academic training. Entry into the program requires students to compete for a place in the second year of the dentistry course through the Health Sciences First Year program. The total duration of the program, including the competitive first year, is five years of full-time academic study. Dentistry in Canada Dentistry in Canada is overseen by the Canadian Dental Association, with specialization regulated by the Royal College of Dentists. Canada has approximately 16,000 dentists. Dental care is not publicly funded, although some provinces provide free dental care for children and the elderly. Most Canadians rely on workplace dental plans or pay out-of-pocket. Historically, dentistry in Canada was rare during the early colonial period, with barbers or blacksmiths performing extractions in severe cases. The first dentists in Canada were United Empire Loyalists fleeing the American Revolution. The first recorded dentist was Mr. Hume, who advertised in Halifax in 1814. Dentistry expanded rapidly in the 19th century, with the Ontario Dental Association forming in 1867 and founding Canada’s first dental school, the Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario, in 1868. The University of Toronto later affiliated with the school. Other Canadian universities subsequently established dental programs, but the University of Toronto remains the largest dental school in Canada, offering extensive postgraduate research opportunities and certifications in all dental specialties. Dental care is not covered by Canada’s public healthcare system. Dentistry in Chile The first dental school in Chile was established at the Universidad de Concepción in 1919. Other institutions offering professional dental education include Universidad de Chile, Universidad de Valparaíso, Universidad de Talca, Universidad Nacional Andrés Bello, Universidad Mayor, Universidad de los Andes, Universidad Diego Portales, and Universidad de Antofagasta. Dentistry in Costa Rica Dentistry in Costa Rica is regulated by the Colegio de Cirujanos Dentistas de Costa Rica. The country is recognized as a leading destination for medical tourism, including dental care, due to its high-quality services and affordability. Dentistry in Iran Dentists in Iran require six years of post-secondary education to earn a Doctor of Dental Surgery (DDS) degree. Those wishing to specialize may pursue further education. Upon graduation, dentists may need to fulfill a two-year military service requirement as dentists in uniform before entering private practice. Notable dental schools include the University of Tehran (School of Dentistry, established in 1939) and the Dental School of Shahid Beheshti University. Dentistry in Italy Dentists in Italy complete five years of undergraduate study to earn their degree. Clinical competencies, such as the surgical removal of a buried tooth root, require a broad range of pre-clinical and clinical knowledge. These competencies are standardized across European Union member states. Dentistry in Malta The University of Malta began offering a degree in Dental Surgery in 1933, with recognition by the UK Medical Council in 1936. Dental Surgery became a separate faculty in 1954. The program admits eight students annually and awards a degree after five years of study. Dentistry in Mexico Dental care in Mexico is significantly less expensive than in many other countries, attracting medical tourists, particularly to cities like Tijuana. However, patients are advised to research providers carefully. Dentistry in Norway Norway offers a five-year dental education program at three universities: the University of Oslo, the University of Bergen, and the University of Tromsø. All dentists in Norway are organized under Tannlegeforeningen. Dental services are free for children. Dentistry in Pakistan Dentistry in Pakistan predates the country’s independence. The de’Montmorency College of Dentistry, established in Lahore in 1934, was the only dental college in the region at the time of partition. Today, Pakistan has over 20 dental schools, both public and private, with approximately 6,200 registered dentists. The Bachelor of Dental Surgery (BDS) degree requires four years of training and a one-year compulsory internship for registration. Dentistry in Slovakia Dentists in Slovakia complete six years of undergraduate study to earn a MUDr (Medicinae Universae Doctor) degree. Dental education is offered at Comenius University in Bratislava and the University of Pavol Jozef Šafárik in Košice. Junior graduates must work under supervision for at least three years to obtain a license from the Slovak Chamber of Dentists. Some dental services are covered by health insurance, but most treatments, such as fillings and prosthodontics, are paid for by patients. Dentistry in Sweden Sweden offers a five-year dental education program at four universities: the University of Malmö, the University of Gothenburg, Karolinska Institutet, and the University of Umeå. Dentists are organized under Tandläkarförbundet, which also publishes the Swedish Dental Journal. Dental care is free for individuals up to 20 years of age. For adults, a fixed state refund covers a portion of the cost, with additional subsidies for expensive treatments for those over 65. Dentistry in the United States Dentistry in the United States is practiced by dentists who have completed a postgraduate professional education program. Dental therapists, who are non-medically trained technicians, are not permitted to practice except in rural Alaska. Dentistry in the U.S. is characterized by high-quality but expensive treatment, with limited access for lower-income populations. Government programs like Medicare and Medicaid generally do not cover routine dental care. Dental education is costly and not federally subsidized, with 56 accredited dental schools requiring four years of postgraduate study. Licensure involves passing national and regional board exams and a state jurisprudence exam. Dentists may pursue additional training in one of nine recognized specialties, such as endodontics, periodontics, or oral surgery. General dentists may perform procedures within these specialties if they are competent, but they are held to the same standards as certified specialists.
